items.title: Sailing along a constant compass bearing draws a spiral around the pole
items.claim: A 'rhumb line' (loxodrome) is a path that crosses every meridian at the same angle — what you sail if you hold a constant compass course. Except for due east/west (the equator) or due north/south, a rhumb line spirals around the pole, eventually reaching it after infinite winding.
items.prompt: Why doesn't a constant bearing give a great circle?

options.text: Great circles change bearing as you traverse them (except along the equator or meridians); to maintain a constant compass bearing, you must follow a different curve that spirals — the loxodrome
It only happens near the pole

items.reveal:
A loxodrome (rhumb line) is the curve that intersects all meridians at the same angle. On a sphere, this is an equiangular spiral.

For any constant bearing not aligned with the equator or a meridian, the path spirals around the pole. The length to reach the pole is finite (the spiral converges) but the number of windings is infinite.

On a Mercator projection, rhumb lines appear as straight lines — this is the property Mercator designed his projection for in 1569. Hold a ruler against a Mercator chart and you have a constant compass bearing course.

Great circles, by contrast, appear as curves on Mercator maps, generally bowed toward the nearer pole. Modern aviation uses great-circle routes; old-school open-ocean sailing used rhumb lines (easier to navigate without constant heading recalculation).

In practice: long-distance navigation often combines them — fly an approximate great circle, but compute waypoints at intervals (e.g., every 5 degrees of longitude) and sail rhumb lines between waypoints. This is 'composite sailing'.

The loxodrome was first studied by the Portuguese navigator Pedro Nunes (1537). It contributed to the systematic mathematisation of navigation in the Age of Discovery.
items.why: Compasses point to magnetic north. Holding a constant bearing draws a curve that no Euclidean intuition prepares you for — and the difference between loxodrome and great circle has shaped maps, navigation, and naval strategy for centuries.

items.title: sin(1 degree) is irrational
items.claim: Sine of 30°, 45°, 60° are simple expressions like 1/2, sqrt(2)/2, sqrt(3)/2. Sine of 1 degree, 7 degrees, or most other 'nice' integer degree values are irrational numbers with no closed elementary form.
items.prompt: Why are most integer-degree sine values irrational?

options.text: Niven's theorem (1956): the only rational values of sin(theta) for rational theta in degrees occur at multiples of 30 (giving sin = 0, plus/minus 1/2, plus/minus 1). Almost all other rational-degree sines are irrational

items.reveal_title: Niven's theorem and the gaps in trigonometric tables
items.reveal:
Ivan Niven (1956) proved: if both theta (in degrees) and sin(theta) are rational, then sin(theta) is 0, ±1/2, or ±1. By similar argument, cos(theta) rational with theta rational forces cos(theta) in {0, ±1/2, ±1, ±sqrt(2)/2... wait — Niven's actual statement covers SINES specifically}.

The consequence: sin(1°), sin(2°), sin(3°), ... are mostly irrational. Specifically, the standard table of integer-degree sines contains only a few rational values: sin(0°) = 0, sin(30°) = 1/2, sin(90°) = 1, and their reflections (150°, 210°, 270°, 330°). Every other entry in the table is irrational.

This is one reason the SPECIAL ANGLES (30°, 45°, 60°) feature so heavily in geometry: they have simple exact values. Most other angles need decimal approximations.

Closed-form expressions: many integer-degree sines do have closed forms in terms of nested radicals — they're algebraic numbers — but the expressions are ugly. For example, sin(15°) = (sqrt(6) - sqrt(2))/4. sin(18°) = (sqrt(5) - 1)/4 (related to the regular pentagon).

For sin(1°): expressible in radicals (it's algebraic, a root of an integer polynomial) but the expression has dozens of nested terms. Modern algebra has tools to compute it exactly; it's just not a useful form.

Why 30° and 45° are special: regular hexagons (60° angles) and squares (45°) tile the plane with simple geometric constructions; the corresponding sine/cosine values come out as simple radicals.

Gauss and constructibility: a regular n-gon is constructible with compass and straightedge if and only if n is a product of powers of 2 and distinct Fermat primes (3, 5, 17, 257, 65537). This is why the 17-gon is constructible (Gauss's first major result, age 19) but the 7-gon and 9-gon aren't.
items.why: Trigonometric tables look like they could be filled with simple values. Almost all entries are deeply irrational, expressible only in nested radicals or numerical approximations. The 'special angles' of school maths are a tiny privileged set.

items.title: Almost every real number is transcendental — but proving it for a specific number is brutal
items.claim: Algebraic numbers (roots of polynomials with integer coefficients) are countable. The reals are uncountable. So almost every real is non-algebraic — transcendental. Yet proving that pi or e is transcendental took heroic effort.
items.prompt: How can almost all numbers have a property that's so hard to verify in specific cases?

options.text: The proofs were just very late

Cardinality arguments tell you transcendental numbers exist abundantly, but don't identify any of them; proving a specific candidate transcendental requires construction of arguments tailored to that number's algebraic relations

items.reveal:
Joseph Liouville (1844) constructed the first known transcendental: sum of 1/10 to the n factorial. The construction was explicit but artificial.

Georg Cantor (1874) showed by counting that the algebraic numbers are countable but the reals are uncountable. Therefore 'most' reals are transcendental, without identifying any.

Charles Hermite (1873) proved e is transcendental — a serious technical achievement.

Ferdinand Lindemann (1882) proved pi is transcendental. This settled the ancient problem of 'squaring the circle': constructing a square with the same area as a given circle, using only compass and straightedge, is impossible because pi is not algebraic.

The Gelfond-Schneider theorem (1934) gave a general criterion: a to the b is transcendental for algebraic a (not 0 or 1) and irrational algebraic b. So 2 to the square root of 2 is transcendental. But e + pi? No one knows. e times pi? No one knows. Even pi + e being irrational remains unproven.

Known transcendentals: e, pi, e to the pi, log 2 (natural log), specific Liouville-style constructions. Unknown: most candidate combinations.
items.why: Generic mathematical truths can be vastly easier to prove than specific instances. 'Most numbers are transcendental' is easy; 'pi is' was a century's work.
